flashcards.back_definition: A virus attaches to a host file and spreads when a person runs or shares that file. A worm spreads by itself across the network by exploiting vulnerabilities, with no user action.
flashcards.back_example: WannaCry jumped between unpatched Windows machines over SMB with nobody clicking anything.
flashcards.back_confusion: The difference changes the defence: user caution slows viruses; patching and closing ports stop worms.
flashcards.back_hook: A virus hitches a ride; a worm drives itself.

flashcards.back_definition: Malware disguised as legitimate software. The user installs it willingly, and it does not copy itself to other machines.
flashcards.back_example: A free "PDF converter" that also installs a remote-access tool.
flashcards.back_confusion: A trojan relies on deception, not self-replication.
flashcards.back_hook: A gift horse full of soldiers.

flashcards.back_definition: It encrypts the victim's files or systems and demands payment for the key. Many groups also steal data first and threaten to leak it (double extortion).
flashcards.back_example: Files renamed to report.docx.locked and a ransom note on the desktop.
flashcards.back_confusion: The files are locked, not deleted. Offline backups remove the attacker's leverage.

flashcards.back_definition: The infection vector is how malware gets in (phishing attachment, USB, unpatched service). The payload is what it does once inside (encrypt, steal, spy).
flashcards.back_example: Vector: a macro in an invoice attachment. Payload: a keylogger.
flashcards.back_confusion: Blocking the vector stops the infection; detecting the payload limits the damage.
flashcards.back_hook: The door it came through vs what it does in the house.

flashcards.front: Why doesn't antivirus catch all malware?
flashcards.back_definition: Signature-based tools only recognise known samples. New, changed or fileless malware can pass until a signature exists; behaviour detection helps but is not perfect.
flashcards.back_example: A freshly repacked sample has a new hash and no signature yet.
flashcards.back_confusion: Defence in depth (patching, backups, least privilege, user awareness) covers what antivirus misses.

flashcards.back_definition: A small device placed between a keyboard and computer that records every keystroke, including passwords.
flashcards.back_example: A thumb-sized adapter on the back of a reception PC's keyboard cable.
flashcards.back_confusion: Software scans cannot see it; physical inspection and tamper seals can.
flashcards.back_hook: Look behind the computer, not just inside it.

flashcards.front: How does a USB Rubber Ducky beat antivirus?
flashcards.back_definition: It pretends to be a keyboard and types pre-programmed commands at high speed. The computer trusts keyboards, so there is no file to scan.
flashcards.back_example: Plugged in for five seconds, it opens PowerShell and downloads a backdoor.
flashcards.back_confusion: Defend with USB device allow-listing, port blockers and never plugging in found drives.
flashcards.back_hook: It doesn't carry a virus; it types one.

flashcards.front: Why is a dropped USB stick dangerous?
flashcards.back_definition: Curiosity makes people plug it in, and the stick can carry malware or act as a keystroke injector.
flashcards.back_example: Stuxnet reached air-gapped Iranian centrifuge systems in 2010 via infected USB drives.
flashcards.back_confusion: An air gap does not protect against what people carry across it.
flashcards.back_hook: Found a USB? Hand it to IT, never to your PC.

flashcards.back_definition: A Trusted Platform Module is a chip that stores encryption keys securely and checks that the boot process has not been changed.
flashcards.back_example: BitLocker uses the TPM to release the disk key only if the boot chain looks untampered.
flashcards.back_confusion: TPM plus full-disk encryption protects a stolen powered-off laptop; a login password alone does not.

flashcards.front: Why are IoT devices such easy targets?
flashcards.back_definition: Default passwords, rarely updated firmware, exposed services such as Telnet or UPnP-opened ports, and huge numbers of identical devices.
flashcards.back_example: Mirai (2016) logged in over Telnet with factory passwords and built a botnet that knocked Dyn's DNS offline.
flashcards.back_confusion: Attackers want the device as a botnet node or a way into your network, not for its own sake.

flashcards.back_definition: Connected devices added to a network without IT's knowledge or approval, so nobody patches or monitors them.
flashcards.back_example: A smart TV in the boardroom joined to the corporate Wi-Fi.
flashcards.back_confusion: You can't secure what you don't know exists: asset inventory comes first.

flashcards.front: What does end-of-life (EOL) mean for a device?
flashcards.back_definition: The vendor no longer releases updates, so any flaw found from now on stays open forever.
flashcards.back_example: An old camera model whose firmware will never be fixed.
flashcards.back_confusion: EOL devices need replacement or compensating controls such as isolation on their own segment.

flashcards.front: Why isn't changing the Wi-Fi password enough to protect IoT devices?
flashcards.back_definition: It controls who joins the network, not whether devices inside trust each other. A device with default admin credentials is still exposed to anything already on the network.
flashcards.back_example: A compromised laptop on the home Wi-Fi logs into the camera with admin/admin.
flashcards.back_confusion: Change each device's own password, update firmware and isolate IoT on a separate network.
flashcards.back_hook: The front gate doesn't lock the rooms.
